solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Mobile yet static in Monaco for instance?

indicators.note: something mobile moves about, so the letters that follow are free to change places

parts.note: the two words taken as written, nine letters in all

explanation.surface: A paradox about Monaco, a place that is both lively and unchanging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' reads as the opposite of 'static', a neat contrast, but it is only the signal to rearrange 'yet static'.
explanation.definitionFit: Monaco is a tiny sovereign country consisting of one urban area, the standard example of an independent city with its own government.

clue.text: Two firms beginning to advertise drink

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, taken twice

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Two companies launch a campaign to promote a beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: CO for company is a standard abbreviation, and 'two' asks for it twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot beverage made from powdered cacao beans mixed with milk or water.

clue.text: Erected film set with alien looking good on screen

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something upright makes it read from the bottom up

parts.note: cine- is the prefix for motion pictures, as in cine camera
to set is to gel, as a jelly does
ET, the film's extra-terrestrial

explanation.surface: A film set is put up for a science-fiction movie featuring an attractive alien.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film set' looks like one noun, a studio stage, but it splits into two pieces; 'Erected' flips the whole chain in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegenic person photographs well and comes across attractively on television or in films.

clue.text: Plain ties and green buckle

indicators.note: to buckle is to bend out of shape, so the letters are distorted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Plain-coloured neckties and a green belt fastening, a note on dull clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like an adjective describing the ties, but it is a noun: a vast flat grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is an enormous grassland region in Tanzania and Kenya, famous for its migrating wildebeest herds.

clue.text: Beater's replacement misusing air rifle hit a cat

indicators.note: misusing something puts it to the wrong use, so these letters are wrongly ordered and need rearranging

parts.note: all fifteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A game beater who shoots a cat with an air rifle gets replaced on the shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: A beater on a shoot flushes birds, which suits the air rifle; here the beater is the organ that beats in the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanical pump implanted to do the work of a failed organ stands in for the thing that beats inside us.

clue.text: Elite Catholic saving good quote about employing a certain force

parts.note: the elect are a chosen elite

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safely held, so one piece holds another

parts.note: Roman as in Roman Catholic
G is the abbreviation for good

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to quote is to cite

explanation.surface: A select group of Catholics keep a favourite quotation about using a particular power.
explanation.walkthrough: Catholic is Roman here, not the usual RC. The definition is the last four words, 'good quote' being two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Electromagnetic devices depend on the combined electric and magnetic interaction, one of the fundamental forces of physics.

clue.text: Join together protecting area in forested country

indicators.note: to protect is to surround and shield, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: to weld is to join metal pieces together
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: An appeal to unite in defence of a wooded region.
explanation.walkthrough: The Weald is an area of south-east England between the North and South Downs, once thickly wooded; the word also means woodland generally.
explanation.definitionFit: Weald is an old word for wooded land, surviving as the name of a once-forested tract of Kent and Sussex.

clue.text: Diameter inside accompanying measurement across

indicators.note: something placed inside is enclosed by what surrounds it

parts.note: accompanying someone is going with them
D is the standard abbreviation for diameter

explanation.surface: A geometry note: the diameter lies within a measurement taken across a shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost literal geometry, which hides that 'Diameter' is only its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Width is the extent of something from side to side, the dimension you take when measuring across it.

clue.text: Stove lit for second time

parts.note: an Aga is a British brand of heavy cast-iron range cooker
a fire that is lit is said to be in

explanation.surface: A stove being lit once more, having gone out.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a British range cooker, usually kept burning; a fire that is still burning is 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something again means repeating it, so it happens another time after the first occasion.

clue.text: Chemist is pounds in red needing turnover

indicators.note: placing something within another means the outer piece surrounds it
turning something over flips it, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
pounds and pens are both enclosures for animals

explanation.surface: A pharmacist is losing money, in the red, and needs more sales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pounds' and 'in red' suggest money, but pounds here are animal enclosures. In Britain a chemist is a pharmacist, one who dispenses medicines.
explanation.definitionFit: A dispensing chemist makes up and hands out prescribed medicines, so both words name the pharmacist doing that job.

clue.text: Miscreant dragging no-good prude into false religion?

indicators.note: putting one thing into another sets it inside

parts.note: a cult is a sect regarded as a false or extreme religion

indicators.note: saying no to something means leaving it out

parts.note: a prig is a smugly moralistic person
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer drags a puritanical person into a bogus sect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No-good' looks like a description of the prude, but it tells you to drop G from PRIG.
explanation.definitionFit: A culprit is the person responsible for a crime or offence, which is what a miscreant or wrongdoer is.

clue.text: Directions given on stop as departing bus is seen?

parts.note: to stop is to end
ways are directions, as in 'which way?'

explanation.surface: Instructions posted at a bus stop as a bus pulls away.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across answer 'on' means after, so the directions follow the stop. The definition is cryptic: a bus driving off shows you its back end.
explanation.definitionFit: Endways means with the end facing forward or toward the viewer, which is how a bus looks as it leaves you behind.

clue.text: Element in legalese judge denied

indicators.note: something denied is refused and taken away, so a letter goes

parts.note: legalese is lawyers' jargon
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A judge is refused a key point buried in legal wording.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing J from JARGON leaves the answer; J for judge appears in law reports, as in Smith J.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is a chemical element, the inert noble gas used to fill light bulbs and make up about one percent of air.

clue.text: Ample opportunity? Hardly

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: a big, plentiful chance
second meaning: an ironic exclamation meaning it is very unlikely

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the idiom means the opposite of its literal words, so the question and its answer contradict each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken literally a fat chance is a large opportunity, but the sarcastic idiom means almost no likelihood at all, like 'hardly'.

clue.text: Cat wants mouse's heart for stuffing as soon as

indicators.note: stuffing is packed inside something, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: 'once you arrive' means as soon as you arrive

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of the word 'mouse'

explanation.surface: A cat craves the insides of a mouse as a filling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat' is the definition, and an unusual one: the ounce is another name for the snow leopard.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is an old name for the snow leopard, a large wild feline of the Central Asian mountains.

clue.text: In Open drive off — hit too far?

indicators.note: one thing being in another means the outer word surrounds it

parts.note: overt means open, not hidden
to shoo is to drive away, as with a cat

explanation.surface: A golfer in the Open tees off and the ball flies past the green.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf picture makes 'Open' the championship and 'drive' a tee shot; really 'Open' is an adjective and 'drive off' means chase away.
explanation.definitionFit: To overshoot is to go past an intended target, as a shot that sails beyond where it was aimed.

clue.text: Intimacy of miss chasing chapter head

indicators.note: one thing chasing another comes behind it, so it is placed afterwards

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for chapter
to miss a chance is to lose it
a ness is a headland, as in Scottish place names

explanation.surface: A romance between a young woman and the head of a chapter house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a young woman, but it is the verb. A ness is a promontory or headland, common in British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Closeness names the state of being emotionally near to someone, a warm familiar bond just like intimacy.

clue.text: Lover no longer criticises one on increase in size

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
a critic pans a play by reviewing it harshly
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former partner mocks someone who has put on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a spiteful ex remarking on weight gain; the pieces simply line up in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Expansion is the act or process of growing larger or spreading out, which is what an increase in size means.

clue.text: Imagine this clue initially turning cryptic!

indicators.note: turning things about changes their arrangement, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters of the words it covers

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: The setter invites you to picture this very clue becoming baffling.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue talks about itself, and the definition doubles as a description of the puzzle genre.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cryptic is mysterious and obscure in meaning, and enigmatic is a direct synonym for puzzling in that way.

clue.text: Woman holds infant fed with a Mexican dish

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: Ena is a woman's name

indicators.note: being fed takes something in, so a piece is inserted

parts.note: an infant is a young child
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mother holds her baby while feeding it Mexican food.
explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions nest, one inside the other; 'Woman' is a first name, a common crossword habit for supplying short letter groups.
explanation.definitionFit: An enchilada is a tortilla rolled round a filling and baked in chilli sauce, a staple of Mexican cooking.

clue.text: Poet in monastery needing year off

indicators.note: 'off' means removed, so the named letter must be taken away

parts.note: a small monastery or convent, run by a senior monk
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A poet living in a monastery wants a sabbatical year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet in monastery' looks like one person, but 'Poet' alone is the definition: Matthew Prior was an English poet around 1700.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew Prior was an English writer of witty verse and a diplomat, so his surname serves as an example of a poet.

clue.text: One having stiff test perhaps taking look round posh home

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: to search is to look for something
U means upper-class, the classic label for posh usage
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: A candidate facing a hard exam visits a grand house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff test' suggests a tough exam, but a test is also the hard shell of an echinoderm; 'perhaps' marks the answer as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea urchin's body is enclosed in a rigid shell of fused plates that biologists call a test, so it is one creature with a hard test.

clue.text: Humble when welcomed to Lincoln?

indicators.note: a guest welcomed to a place is taken in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln's nickname
'as' can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: A modest person received by the city of Lincoln, or perhaps by the president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lincoln' could be the English cathedral city or the president; it is the president, known as Honest Abe.
explanation.definitionFit: To humble someone is to lower their pride or dignity, and abase is a verb meaning to degrade or belittle in that way.

clue.text: Washing cycle showing movable energy controls

indicators.note: the symbol for energy is movable, so that single letter shifts to a new spot and the order changes

parts.note: a rinse cycle is part of a washing machine's programme

explanation.surface: A washing machine's cycle displays adjustable power settings.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the E moves: shift it from fourth to second place in RINSE and the answer appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Reins are the straps a rider uses to steer a horse, and figuratively the reins are the means of control over something.

clue.text: Wanderer bathes old woman in green light

indicators.note: bathing someone immerses them, so one piece is surrounded by another
placed in something means enclosed by it

parts.note: a nod and a green light both mean approval to go ahead
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A traveller washes an elderly woman under a green-tinted lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old woman' is slang for one's mother, hence MA; 'green light' is permission rather than a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad has no fixed home and roams from place to place, so a wanderer is exactly such a roving person.

clue.text: Live and prosper where nothing is sacrificed

indicators.note: what is sacrificed is given up, so a letter is lost

parts.note: to prosper is to do well
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A motto for thriving without giving anything up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live and prosper' echoes the Star Trek greeting, which hides that 'Live' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere is to reside or have your home there, which is one sense of the verb live.

clue.text: Old clubs song involving new instrument

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one piece is placed inside

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
an aria is a solo song in an opera
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: An old club anthem is played with a novel musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like club singing; it is a string of standard abbreviations with N slipped inside the song.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocarina is a small egg-shaped wind instrument with finger holes, usually made of clay.

clue.text: Man's between dry lake's shores to see plant

indicators.note: something between two things sits in the gap, so it goes inside

parts.note: TT means teetotal, someone who abstains from alcohol
a man's things are his

indicators.note: shores are the edges of water, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of 'lake'

explanation.surface: A man stands between the banks of a dried-up lake to look at a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' means teetotal here, TT, not waterless; the lake's shores are its two outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A thistle is a prickly plant with purple flower heads, and the emblem of Scotland.

clue.text: River claiming last of Olympian youth

indicators.note: to claim something is to take it into your possession, so one piece holds another

parts.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A river takes the life of a young Olympic athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tees is a river in north-east England, flowing out at Middlesbrough.
explanation.definitionFit: The teens are the ages from thirteen to nineteen, the period of life known as youth or adolescence.

clue.text: Catch with line at sea in accordance with strict rules

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and all over the place, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An angler fishing offshore with a line, following the rules exactly.
explanation.walkthrough: The fishing picture makes 'at sea' literal; it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Technical means according to a strict or literal interpretation of the rules, as in a technical foul or a technical knockout.
